pedagogy.summary: Interpret and construct pie charts as proportions of one whole. Convert each category count to its fraction of the total and then to a sector angle: (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Recover a count from an angle only when the total is known. Move between the table, fraction/percentage, sector angle and constructed circle; check calculations and drawing rather than relying only on whether the sectors total 360°.
bestPractices: Establish the pie chart as parts of ONE whole: the full circle (360°) is the whole data set, and each sector is that category's fraction of it — so a sector shows a proportion, never a raw count

Teach sector angles as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, and always check both that the sectors sum to 360° and that each sector matches its table fraction; explicitly contrast with the wrong 'divide 360 by the frequency' and 'multiply frequency by the total' methods
To read an actual quantity from a pie chart, combine the sector (its angle/fraction) with the KNOWN total — make explicit that the raw frequency is not shown on the chart itself
Connect pie-chart angles to percentages and to the angles-at-a-point fact (360°), so children draw on proportion and angle knowledge together
Move fluently in both directions — table → angles → chart to construct, and chart + total → quantities to interpret — so the representation and the data stay linked
keyRepresentations: A circle as the whole (360°) partitioned into sectors, each labelled with its fraction/percentage of the total
The formula (frequency ÷ total) × 360° shown alongside a data table being turned into sectors
A protractor laying off each sector angle from a starting radius (the construction act)
A double representation — same data as a table and as a pie chart — to move between proportion and count
commonMisconceptions: Reading a pie sector as a raw quantity rather than a proportion of the whole — or trying to read an actual count off the chart without using the total
Calculating a sector angle by dividing 360° by the frequency (instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°)
Calculating a sector angle by multiplying the frequency by the total frequency
Not checking that the sector angles sum to 360°

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, interpret and construct pie charts. The full 360° circle is one data set; each sector angle is the category fraction of the total multiplied by 360°. Recover a count by multiplying the sector fraction by the known total. Compute the angles, draw them with a protractor, label categories, and verify each against the table as well as checking their sum. This topic does not assess line-graph mastery, which belongs to the separate Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp).

activities.title: Live pie-chart builder from class data
feedback: If the sectors do not exactly fill the circle (leaving a gap or overlapping), at least one angle is wrong — check the method and the arithmetic: each angle should be the category's fraction of the whole, taken of 360°

360 ÷ 12 = 30° (with 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) makes the sectors total only 150° — less than half the circle — so the circle itself shows the angle must be a fraction of 360°, not 360 divided by the count
After computing, total the sector angles: if they do not make 360°, find the error before drawing
The 'show actual numbers' toggle needs the total because a sector shows only a proportion — an unlabelled sector does not show the raw count on its own
activities.rationale: Construction forces the proportional idea into the open: a live repartitioning circle links the computed angle to a visible share and lets wrong methods fall visibly short of the whole circle, while the protractor step performs the actual construction act. The greyed-out count toggle makes 'sector = proportion, not count' explicit.
sourceClaims: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°

In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Enter a class data table into a tool that repartitions a circle in real time, e.g. favourite pet: dog 12, cat 6, rabbit 6, with 24 children in all
Watch dog's 12-out-of-24 sector swing open to fill exactly half the circle, with a label ticking over to 180° and 50%
Compute each sector angle yourself as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°: dog 12/24 × 360° = 180°, cat and rabbit 6/24 × 360° = 90° each
Add the sector angles and confirm they sum to 360° before drawing

Deliberately try the tempting wrong method 360 ÷ 12 = 30° for dog (and 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) and watch the sectors fall well short of closing, totalling only 150° and leaving 210° of the circle empty
Use a protractor-construction mode to lay off each computed angle from a starting radius
Use a 'show actual numbers' toggle that stays greyed out until the total is entered, making visible that a sector is a proportion, not a count
activities.intendedInsight: A pie sector's angle is the category's share of the whole circle — (frequency ÷ total) × 360° — not 360 divided by the frequency and not frequency times the total; and the sectors must sum to one whole turn, 360°.

activities.title: Recover a count from a sector and the total
feedback: Answering '90 children walk' reads the angle as a count — 90° is the angle, not the number of children
The whole circle is all 40 children; a right angle is a quarter of the circle, so a quarter of 40 = 10
Saying 'you cannot tell' misses that the total lets you recover the count — fraction of the whole × total
activities.rationale: Separating the angle/fraction from the count via the total directly confronts the sector-as-quantity misconception and makes the role of the total explicit.
sourceClaims: In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Read a given pie chart where a sector's angle is stated, e.g. 'the walk sector is a right angle, 90°, and 40 children travel in all — how many walk?'
Work out the sector's fraction of the whole: 90° is a quarter of 360°, so a quarter of 40 = 10 children walk
Try a second: 'a sector is 72° and there are 20 children altogether — how many is that?' (72/360 × 20 = 4)
State explicitly which number came from the chart (the angle/fraction) and which from the given total (the count)
activities.intendedInsight: To get an actual quantity from a pie chart you must combine the sector's fraction with the known total; the raw count is not visible on the chart itself.

activities.title: Compare same-size sectors from different totals
feedback: Equal slice sizes mean equal fractions, not equal counts — apply each chart's own total
Recover each count separately: the same fraction of different totals gives different numbers (a third of 30 = 10, a third of 12 = 4)
When a fraction of a total is not a whole number of people, re-check the data or the fraction; counts of people must be whole
activities.rationale: A counterexample with two totals tests whether the child treats a sector as a proportion rather than an absolute quantity, reinforcing the proportion-plus-total move.
sourceClaims: In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Compare two pie charts: a class of 30 and a class of 12 that both have a 'football' sector of the same size (say 120°, a third of the circle)
Decide whether the equal-size slices mean the same number of children, and justify
Work out the two actual counts using each chart's own total: a third of 30 = 10 versus a third of 12 = 4, noticing that equal fractions give different counts
activities.intendedInsight: A sector is a proportion of ITS OWN total; equal-looking sectors from different totals can represent different counts.

activities.title: Scorable checks on interpret and partial-construct skills
feedback: Choosing the '360 ÷ frequency' option usually gives sectors that do not total 360°, and even when the total happens to come out right it is not the category's fraction of the whole — the fraction-of-360 method, (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, is correct
If the fill-in count is wrong, check whether you used the total and the sector's fraction together
A correct interpretation or angle calculation is a start; construct a complete pie chart to demonstrate the drawing skill
activities.rationale: Short response formats give a scorable check of interpretation and part of construction; because choosing a correct angle is recognition rather than building, pair them with the full builder.
sourceClaims: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
learnerActions: Complete a fill-in task: 'the bus sector is 120°, there are 36 children, so ___ take the bus' (12)
Compute a sector angle from a table in a single step and enter it
Answer a multiple-choice item that includes the '360 ÷ frequency' answer as a tempting wrong option, and explain why it is wrong
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a sector with the total and computing a sector angle can be checked for accuracy; recognising a correct angle is not the same as constructing a whole chart.

activities.title: Annotated reference charts for reviewing structure
feedback: Use the revealed labels to check your own work, then redo an unlabelled example to confirm you can do it unaided
Reading a labelled chart does not show you can build one — follow up with construction
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart with reveals is a useful reference and worked example, but it does not elicit independent construction or exercise the proportional reasoning that discriminates understanding, so it supports rather than replaces building.
learnerActions: On a labelled pie chart, reveal each sector's angle, fraction/percentage and — given the total — its count, to confirm how the three relate
Use these as worked examples when checking your own constructions or interpretations
activities.intendedInsight: Relating the angle, fraction and count on an annotated pie chart can support review, but independent construction must be checked separately.

constraints: Response-format checks (fill-in, multiple choice, slider) can assess interpretation and approximate construction by choosing a correct angle, but choosing an angle is recognition, not building; pair them with an activity where the child constructs the full chart.
Annotated/static charts with reveals serve as reference and worked examples; they do not elicit independent construction or exercise the proportional reasoning that discriminates understanding.
Use a flat pie chart; 3D perspective or an exploded view can distort the areas learners compare as proportions.

In-role dialogue does not elicit the drawing/construction act — laying off sector angles with a protractor and producing a finished chart to inspect — so it cannot demonstrate the construction skill, even though a child could narrate a calculation in dialogue; it is not a substitute for the compute-and-draw work.
When recovering counts, use data sets and sector fractions that give whole numbers of people where the context is people, so learner answers stay coherent.
Connect pie-chart angles to percentages and to the angles-at-a-point fact (the full turn is 360°) so proportion and angle knowledge reinforce each other.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original counterexample compared a 'football' sector of equal size in classes of 30 and 12 without fixing the angle. A quarter would give 7.5 children for the class of 30 (not a whole number), so the activity now uses a third (120°), giving whole counts of 10 and 4 while still demonstrating that equal fractions of different totals give different counts.

'Show the wrong methods failing' is presented as an observable property of the circle not closing (the wrong angles total 180°, about half the circle); this is a reasonable visual argument, but the claim that watching it fail uniquely corrects the misconception is not established by the cited sources and has been softened.

The claim about in-role dialogue was narrowed from 'cannot verify calculation' to the observable limit that it does not elicit the drawing/construction act or a finished chart; a child could still narrate a calculation in dialogue.

probeDeeper: 'Why does apple get 180° when only 10 children chose it?' — pushes the proportion (10 out of 20 is half the whole circle) into words
Two classes have 120° football sectors: one class has 30 children and the other has 12. How many chose football in each class, and why do equal sector angles not imply equal counts?
'A sector is 72° and there are 20 children altogether — how would you find how many that is?' — checks angle → fraction → count via the total
Can sector angles total 360° even if the category shares are wrong? Explain why you must also check every sector against the table.
assess.correctAnswer: The walk sector is 90/360 = 1/4 (25%) of the whole, so 1/4 × 60 = 15 children walk. For the fruit chart: apple 10/20 = 1/2 (50%), so 10/20 × 360° = 180°; banana and orange are each 5/20 = 1/4 (25%), so 5/20 × 360° = 90° each. The angles total 360° and each sector agrees with its table fraction. A completed labelled drawing is required for construction; computing or selecting an angle alone does not demonstrate the full skill.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sector-as-quantity: reads a pie sector's angle as a raw count, or tries to read an actual number off the chart without using the total — not treating the sector as a proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: the whole circle is all 60 children; a right angle is a quarter of the circle, so a quarter of 60; the sector shows a share, and the count needs the total
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On interpret (a) the child answers '90 children walk' (reading the angle as a count) or says you cannot tell, rather than a quarter of 60 = 15

errorPatterns.pattern: Angle = 360 ÷ frequency: computes each sector angle by dividing 360° by the category's frequency, instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the proportion via the percentages/proportion prerequisite: the angle is the category's SHARE of the whole — (frequency ÷ total) × 360° — and the shares must add up to the full circle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On construction the child writes 360 ÷ 10 = 36° for apple (or multiplies frequency by the total); the sectors do not fill or sum to 360°

errorPatterns.pattern: No 360° check: constructs sectors without verifying they sum to a whole turn, so errors go unnoticed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: add the checking habit — total the sector angles and confirm 360° before drawing; the proportional idea is intact
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child's method is broadly right but the drawn/calculated sectors sum to more or less than 360° and they do not notice

responseLevels.gap: Treats an angle as a count or cannot relate a category fraction to its share of 360°.
responseLevels.full: Uses the total to recover counts and independently constructs and labels a correct pie chart from a fresh table, checking each fraction and the angle sum.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given sector and computes a familiar angle but needs support to calculate, draw or check the entire chart.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First interpret: a pie chart represents 60 children and its walk sector is 90°. How many children walk? Then construct: a table has apple 10, banana 5 and orange 5, total 20. Calculate every sector angle, draw the pie chart with a protractor, label the categories, and explain how you checked it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 90° interpretation requires using the total rather than reading the angle as a count. The construction task distinguishes calculation and recognition from producing a correctly partitioned chart. Wrong rules are checked against category shares, not only the angle sum, because an incorrect construction can still total 360°.
